extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters / patent attorneys / patent applicants drafting claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for drafting patent claims (product, process, use, medical indication, composition, biotechnology, and computer-implemented claims) and strategic claim-set design across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define a product in terms of the process by which it is made (product-by-process claims) are still directed to the product as such and confer absolute protection on that product; a product is not typically rendered novel merely because it is made by means of a new process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a product-by-process claim defines a product by its method of manufacture, to meet the novelty requirement the claimed product must not be identical to a known product. The burden of proving allegedly distinguishing product-by-process features lies with the applicant, who must provide evidence (e.g., differences in the properties of the products) that modification of process parameters results in a different product. In jurisdictions such as the EPO the purpose of the process is also considered when determining product features; in most jurisdictions protection extends to products directly obtained by the process (even for superficial changes). Some jurisdictions treat product-by-process claims as method claims or find them indefinite (e.g., Japan). Professional tip: check whether product-by-process is permissible and the best approach in the target jurisdiction and consider it as part of a mix of claim formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty standard for product-by-process
rubrics_metrics.description: For novelty, a product defined by process must not be identical to a known product; process-based drafting does not automatically impart novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must demonstrate that the process-derived product differs from prior art products by objective, verifiable properties. Be prepared to supply testable evidence and to anticipate examiner scrutiny that a process-based definition might disguise lack of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define inventions by parameters (characteristic values or mathematical formulae) are allowed where the invention cannot otherwise be adequately defined without unduly restricting claim scope, provided parameters are objectively and directly verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the claimed parameters are measurable and can be directly and positively verified without undue experimentation by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description or known to the person skilled in the art. The EPO allows parameter characterization when necessary and requires parameters to be clearly and reliably determinable by indications in the description or by objective procedures usual in the art. Be aware examiners may scrutinize parameter claims for disguised lack of novelty. Provide specification directions (test procedures, reference standards) to enable routine verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: General use claims (non-medical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use claims assert protection for a new and inventive use of a product (a subtype of process claim); in some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) a nonmedical use claim such as 'use of substance X as an insecticide' is accepted and treated as equivalent to a process claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a 'use of X as Y' claim will be treated as a product claim. In jurisdictions that accept such use claims they will be interpreted as process claims (e.g., 'a process of killing insects using substance X'), and they should not be read as product claims directed to the product per se. Check local practice as some countries (notably the United States) do not recognize 'use' as a statutory claim category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical indication claims and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: For new medical uses of known products, multiple claim formats exist (Swiss-type claims, purpose-limited product claims, use claims, substance-when-used claims, and method of treatment claims) and national laws and practice vary significantly as to permissibility and the protection conferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the appropriate format(s) for each jurisdiction. Examples given: Swiss-type ('use of X in the manufacture of a medicament for treatment of Y'), purpose-limited product claims ('X for use in the treatment of Y' — EPO compulsory since 2011), use claims (accepted in countries like Germany, Canada, Australia), 'substance when used' claims, and method-of-treatment claims (accepted in US and Australia). The patentability and enforcement (e.g., who is a direct infringer, exemptions for medical practitioners) differ among countries. Professional tip: ensure the priority application's description supports selection of the most appropriate claim formats for later filings; include multiple formats where strategic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple claim types for comprehensive protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft a set of claims containing various claim types (product, use/medical-indication, process/preparation, method) so that if one claim type is invalidated another may still provide protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a product claim is novel and nonobvious, related use and process claims will generally be considered novel; nonetheless, include product, use and process claims where appropriate to comprehensively protect the invention and mitigate risk. Example: include product claim for Product X, general/first medical use claim, specific medical-use claim, and a preparation process claim. Be mindful of differing national rules that may affect which claim types are necessary or effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims — element-level breadth choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition claims describe the chemical nature or components of an invention; drafters may claim elements as narrowly or broadly as necessary in view of prior art and business objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide element-by-element whether to specify exact compounds or use generic, functional wording (e.g., 'a pH-modifying substrate in an amount sufficient to adjust pH to 3.5–5.0') depending on novelty, scope desired, and prior art. A generically-stated element can encompass many alternatives (risk of overbreadth vs enforceability). Draft depending on whether you wish to capture any compound that performs the stated function or a specific identified chemical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology claims — sequence listings and deposit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotechnology inventions (cDNA, recombinant DNA, proteins, monoclonal antibodies, microorganisms, cultivars, etc.) may require special claim formats, sequence listings and deposit of biological material where words alone cannot adequately describe how to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where access to biological material is necessary for enablement, use the deposit system (Budapest Treaty) and include deposit references (e.g., ATCC accession numbers) in the application. Ensure compliance with national sequence-listing rules and deposit requirements; include adequate disclosure in the specification and follow deposit formalities to ensure the material is available for patent procedures across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented invention claims and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas, software or computer programs 'as such', pure mental acts and business methods as such are excluded from patentable subject matter in many jurisdictions; acceptable claim formats include apparatus/product, method/process, use claims, computer-readable medium (Beauregard), data-structure (Lowry) and other jurisdiction-specific forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a mix of claim types: method claims often capture dynamic algorithmic behavior (common as Claim 1), and product/apparatus claims should also be included. In jurisdictions that permit referring a product claim to method claims, a product claim can refer back to method claims; where such referencing is not allowed, rephrase method steps into apparatus 'means for …' language or specific functional language. Beware that 'means for' claim language has different interpretations by jurisdiction (e.g., US means-plus-function claim rules). Consider specialized formats (computer-readable medium claims, data-structure claims, propagated signal claims) appropriate to target jurisdictions. Professional tip: keep up to date with evolving national practice for software/CIIs and choose claim formats strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting order — prepare the claims first
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin drafting a patent application by preparing the claims first because doing so helps refine the inventive concept and guides the description and other parts of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the physical embodiment as a starting point but iteratively abstract and broaden the claim language to capture the inventive concept. Drafting claims first aids in identifying essential versus non-essential features and helps structure dependent claims and fallback positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad and narrow claims — build a claim set from broadest to narrowest
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft a combination of broad and narrow claims to capture the full scope of an invention's novelty; an ideal claim set ranges from the broadest feasible claim to the narrowest dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical approach is to start with a narrow claim and incrementally remove or generalize elements to arrive at the broadest allowable claim, then draft dependent claims from it. Use dependent claims to reintroduce omitted elements as fallback positions. Ensure each claim legitimately captures novel and nonobvious subject matter and avoid introducing non-novel elements that do not contribute to inventive step in the broadest claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent claim sets and alternative focuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Include multiple independent claim sets (e.g., apparatus/product, element-specific device, method/process, full-process) focusing on different aspects or alternative points of novelty of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft independent claim sets when each truly represents independent novelty or when the prior art is unclear. Use dependent claims within each set to recover features removed during broadening. Avoid creating alternative sets solely for the sake of alternatives unless they represent commercially significant distinct novelties; excessive trivial alternatives can draw examiner objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align claim scope with inventor's objectives and commercial strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalizing breadth, ensure the claims reflect the inventor's or applicant's commercial intentions and the likely scope of use/enforcement; do not automatically maximize breadth contrary to client wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What are the goals of this invention? Who/what is likely to infringe? To whom could the patent be licensed? Is broad protection commercially desirable or risky? If the inventor envisions a very narrow, specific application, draft narrower claims; if broader adaptation is anticipated, draft broader claims but ensure each broader claim is supportable and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness, claim count and claim drafting practicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions require that claims be 'concise' and may object to undue repetition, many trivial claims, or multiple alternatives within a single claim that obscure scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid undue repetition between claims by using dependent claim form. Be mindful of what constitutes a reasonable number of claims in the target jurisdiction and avoid submitting many trivial variations that invite examiner objection. Do not present multiple alternatives within one claim in a way that obscures the claim's scope; where necessary, create separate dependent or independent claims for meaningful alternatives.
